description_full: YETI Holdings, Inc. designs, retails, and distributes outdoor products under the YETI brand name in the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Europe, and Japan. It offers hard coolers, including the YETI Tundra, YETI Roadie, YETI V Series hard coolers, YETI TANK ice bucket, and YETI Silo 6G water cooler, as well as related accessories comprising locks, dry baskets, beverage holders, and dividers. The company also provides soft cooler bags, such as under the Hopper collection and Daytrip collection; duffel bags, backpacks, luggage, and packing cubes comprising the Panga collection, Crossroads collection, Camino Caryall, SideKick Dry gear case, Cayo collection, and Ranchero collection; cargo and storage solutions that include the LoadOut GoBox, LoadOut bucket, and LoadOut swivel seat names; and outdoor living products, which consist of Trailhead camp chair, Lowlands blanket, Boomer dog bowls, Hondo beach chair, can crusher, and the YETI Fire Pit. In addition, it offers bottles and jugs under the Rambler, Yonder, and Silo collections; cups, mugs, and tumblers under the Rambler collection; Rambler products, including tableware, coffeeware, barware, and containers, as well as insulated bowls and food jars, ceramic-lined mugs and stackable cups, French presses, pitchers, wine chillers, wine tumblers, the beverage bucket, colsters, and cocktail shakers; and cookware. Further, the company provides apparel, such as hats, shirts, and sweatshirts, as well as ice substitutes and other YETI branded products. It sells its products through its direct-to-consumer channel, including websites, corporate sales programs, and retail stores, as well as through its wholesale channel. YETI Holdings, Inc. was founded in 2006 and is headquartered in Austin, Texas.
ceo_bio: Mr. Matthew J. Reintjes | President, CEO & Chairman | Age 50 | Compensation: $2.2M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 1K people. Revenue per employee of $1.3M ranks in the top quartile among Consumer Cyclical peers, improving at 13%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $153K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $34K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 2× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (2/10).
financial_summary: YETI Holdings, Inc. is a mid-cap consumer cyclical business with a $3.3B market cap on $1.9B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +5% over the past three years, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 23% against a 11% cost of capital — a 12-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 57% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $212M in free cash flow — roughly 11 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.54× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.3× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 45× is fortress-like.

Management returns a meaningful 9.1% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 11% operating margin is roughly in line with the Consumer Cyclical median (8%).
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.38x).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-13.7% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 15% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 10% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 17% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 41% and a beta of 1.29, it amplifies market moves, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.75 vs 5y 1.45), so read it loosely.
About $66.6M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 59% in the 2020 crash and 65% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades only 6% below its DCF fair value of $47.69, a thin margin of safety.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 1%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $34.86 to $66.56 (P10-P90).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 16% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 6.5% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.9% (vs the 8% bar).
The 16 covering analysts target $54.06 on average, 20% above the price.
The price implies 10.9% annual cash-flow growth, 1pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 23% clears the cost of capital of 11.0% by 12pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.35).
It runs a 57% gross margin and converts 11% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.54x.
ROE of 25% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.9x equity multiplier).
It spends 1.3% of revenue on R&D and 2.6% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.3x net debt to EBITDA ($59.8M of cash against $72.5M of debt), with interest covered 45.0x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 6.6, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 5.4% over 3 years and 11.3% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded -9.6% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs only 0.8x depreciation (2.3% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 20, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.7%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
It returns 9.1% a year to shareholders (9.1% in buybacks).
The share count has shrunk 3.6% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
Short interest is elevated at 12.6% of the float, 4.0 days to cover.
people: With about 1,390 employees, each generates about $1.3M of revenue, 3.5x the Consumer Cyclical median, and productivity has risen 13.3% a year.
That works out to $153K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.2M (2x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
